sections.markdown:
## C — Front and rear no zones, trucks on hills and in turns, meeting and turning near trucks, yielding to emergency vehicles, what to do at a traffic stop, the move-over law and slow-moving, farm and animal-drawn vehicles
Knowledge domain: how a South Carolina driver stays clear of large trucks and buses in front, behind and in turns, makes way for emergency vehicles, behaves safely and lawfully when stopped by law enforcement, follows the move-over law and passes slow-moving, farm and animal-drawn vehicles.

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A01
A loaded truck with good tires and properly adjusted brakes, in ideal conditions at 55 mph, needs at least 335 feet to stop, more than 1½ times a car's stopping distance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A01
Because trucks stop so slowly, never pull onto a road or change lanes in front of a large vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A01
When passing a large vehicle, wait until its whole front shows in your rearview mirror before moving in front of it, and keep up your speed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A01
Unlike cars, large vehicles have huge blind spots directly behind them that reach up to 200 feet. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A02
Do not follow a large vehicle too closely, and position your vehicle so its driver can see you in the side mirrors. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A02
On steep hills, up or down, large vehicles must travel slowly, about 35 mph, and so they use the right lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A02
Where possible, stay out of the right lane on hills and near truck weigh stations, where trucks try to re-enter faster traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A02
To turn right, a truck or bus driver may first swing wide to the left, sometimes using space from other lanes, to clear the curb corner. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A02
Never try to slip between a turning truck or bus and the curb, where you could be squeezed into a serious collision; wait until it has finished its turn. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A03
When meeting a truck from the opposite direction, keep as far right as you can to avoid a sideswipe and to reduce the wind turbulence that pushes the two vehicles apart. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A03
Many large-vehicle collisions happen at intersections when drivers misjudge an approaching truck's speed before turning left, so if in doubt, do not turn left in its path. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A03
Stop lines set you farther back at an intersection so larger vehicles have more room to turn, so always stop behind them. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A03
Never cut off a large vehicle, whether to make your exit or turn or to get ahead of a truck before a single-lane construction zone, because saving a few seconds is not worth a life. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A04
When an emergency vehicle has its flashing lights and siren on, yield by pulling over to the edge of the road so it can pass, and try not to block intersections, roads or driveways. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A04
When you see emergency lights behind you, stay calm, turn on your signal and pull to the side of the road as soon as you safely can. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A04
Once stopped, turn off the ignition and radio, switch on your hazard flashers and stay in your vehicle unless the officer tells you to get out. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A04
Keep your hands on the steering wheel where they are easy to see, and have passengers stay calm, stay belted in the vehicle and keep their hands in plain view. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A04
Neither you nor your passengers should use phones or other devices, and do not make sudden movements or dig for your license or papers before the officer gives instructions. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A04
If there are any weapons in the vehicle, tell the officer about all of them at first contact, and concealed weapons permit holders should follow their CWP procedures. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0120]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A05
Roll down your window to talk with the officer, and if the officer is in an unmarked vehicle or not in uniform, ask to see law enforcement credentials. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A05
The officer may ask for your driver's license, proof of insurance and vehicle registration, and if they are out of reach, say where they are and ask before reaching for them. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A05
The officer may issue a warning or a traffic ticket that may include a fine, and if you disagree, do not argue at the roadside, because you can explain your side in court. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A05
Accepting a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A05
South Carolina does not require a driver to sign a traffic ticket, but in another state refusing to sign may lead to arrest under that state's laws. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0121]

FACT_ID: sec14-F25 | anchor: A06
If an officer believes a crime has been committed, the officer may search your vehicle without a court-issued warrant as long as there is probable cause. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec14-F26 | anchor: A06
Never try to flee from law enforcement, since police chases cause many deadly collisions and the penalties for fleeing are worse than any original traffic citation. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec14-F27 | anchor: A06
Because more and more responders and tow truck operators are being struck on the road, South Carolina has a move-over law requiring drivers to slow down and change lanes when approaching emergency vehicles. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0122]

FACT_ID: sec14-F28 | anchor: A07
When approaching a stopped authorized emergency vehicle, proceed with caution, slow down and yield by changing into a lane away from it if safety and traffic allow. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec14-F29 | anchor: A07
If changing lanes away from a stopped emergency vehicle is unsafe, slow down and continue with caution at a speed that is safe for traffic conditions. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec14-F30 | anchor: A07
Watch for slow-moving vehicles, especially in rural areas. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0123]

FACT_ID: sec14-F31 | anchor: A08
A fluorescent or reflective orange and red triangle on the back of a farm, construction or animal-drawn vehicle means it travels at less than 25 mph, so approach with care and pass only when it is safe. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec14-F32 | anchor: A08
Tractors, combines and other farm equipment cross roads and travel on rural state highways, and their operators most likely cannot hear approaching vehicles over the machinery noise, so pass with caution. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec14-F33 | anchor: A08
Animal-drawn vehicles and horseback riders have the same right to use the road as motor vehicles, must follow the same rules and can suffer heavy damage and injury if hit. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

FACT_ID: sec14-F34 | anchor: A08
Pass animal-drawn vehicles and riders with caution, do not honk or rev your engine, which may scare the animal, and expect them to make left turns into fields and driveways. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0124]

Misconceptions: never cut in front of a large vehicle, because it needs far longer to stop than a car; being close behind a truck does not make you visible to its driver; a truck swinging left may be about to turn right; refusing to sign a ticket is lawful in South Carolina but may lead to arrest elsewhere; a stopped emergency vehicle calls for moving over or slowing, not just passing at normal speed.
Mnemonics: about three hundred thirty-five feet for a loaded truck to stop from fifty-five, a rear no zone up to two hundred feet; if you cannot see the driver in the mirror, the driver cannot see you; at a stop, engine off, flashers on, hands on the wheel; orange and red triangle, under twenty-five.
Glossary: front no zone means the area just ahead of a large vehicle, which it needs to stop; rear no zone means the large blind spot directly behind a large vehicle; weigh station means a roadside truck site from which large vehicles re-enter faster traffic; probable cause means the grounds that let an officer who believes a crime was committed search a vehicle without a warrant; move-over law means the rule to change lanes away from, or slow for, a stopped emergency vehicle; slow-moving vehicle triangle means the orange and red triangle on vehicles traveling under twenty-five miles per hour.

corpus_stability.reason: The South Carolina Driver's Manual prints a single edition line (Revised 06/2024) on its front cover; its disclaimer says legislative and SCDMV policy changes may make some content out of date until the agency incorporates them, and a possibly newer unlinked upload exists on the issuer site (freshness debt in the run jams), so the corpus is treated as revised at most about once a year, bound to the registered snapshot.
